REFERENCE / MOTION / 22 SEP 2026

What the damping
ratio changes.

Three behaviours, one equation. A companion to the spring experiment.

ON THIS PAGE
A useful distinctionThree regimesIn a gameThe equation

A useful distinction

Stiffness and damping do different jobs. Stiffness pulls the spring towards its target. Damping resists velocity and removes energy from the motion.

The damping ratio, ζ, describes damping relative to the critical amount. In this experiment the mass and natural frequency stay fixed, so changing ζ isolates one behaviour.

Three regimes

ζ < 1 / Underdamped
The response overshoots the target and oscillates around it. Less damping means more persistent oscillation.
ζ = 1 / Critically damped
The fastest return without oscillation for this linear spring starting at rest after a step in the target.
ζ > 1 / Overdamped
No oscillation, but a slower approach. Increasing damping further makes the response more sluggish.

Compare all three in the lab →

In a game

For a camera, a little overshoot can be expressive. For a small interface adjustment, the same overshoot might make the control feel imprecise. The right behaviour depends on what the player needs to follow.

A graph helps compare settings, but it can’t tell you how a moving target, collision, or camera transition will feel in context. That still needs testing in the actual scene.

The equation

x″ + 2ζωx′ + ω²x = ω² · target

Here x is position, x′ is velocity, x″ is acceleration, and ω is natural frequency. This version sets mass to one. The lab uses an exact solution for a fixed target step, rather than an approximate frame-by-frame simulation.

Reference: OpenStax — Damped Oscillations. The interactive model is in spring-model.js.
